chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
On September 20, 2024, Constellation Energy Corporation set a marker for the entire US merchant-power sector. The company announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft Corporation for the entire 835-megawatt output of Three Mile Island Unit 1 — the storied Pennsylvania reactor that had sat idle since 2019 — which it rechristened the Crane Clean Energy Center, honouring former Exelon chief executive Chris Crane. At 835 megawatts of carbon-free baseload capacity delivered under a dedicated bilateral contract to the world's largest enterprise software company, the deal crystallised a thesis the power markets had been pricing tentatively: that AI data centre load growth represents a new class of electricity demand capable of funding the resurrection of dormant nuclear infrastructure. Constellation's equity, trading as CEG on the NASDAQ, advanced sharply in the days following the announcement, cementing a re-rating that had been building since the Inflation Reduction Act's passage but now found its commercial proof of concept.

## Company Profile

Constellation Energy Corporation (CEG, NASDAQ) is headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland. It is the largest nuclear power generator in the United States, operating approximately 22 gigawatts of nuclear capacity across 12 plants and more than 21 reactors — among them Byron, Braidwood, Calvert Cliffs, Clinton, Dresden, Ginna, LaSalle, Limerick, Nine Mile Point, Peach Bottom, Quad Cities, and the Crane Clean Energy Center. Around that nuclear core sits a smaller portfolio of gas, hydro, wind, and solar generation, plus a competitive retail and wholesale power supply business spanning PJM, MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE.

The company was formed through the February 1, 2022 spin-off from Exelon Corporation, which retained the regulated utility subsidiaries — ComEd, PECO, BGE, Pepco, Delmarva, and ACE. Joseph Dominguez, who had led ComEd within the Exelon structure, was named president and chief executive of the newly independent company. Daniel Eggers, who joined as chief financial officer in December 2021, anchored the finance function through the separation and the post-spin capital deployment programme. Non-executive Chairman Mayo Shattuck III — who served as chairman, president, and chief executive of the original Constellation Energy Group and led its 2012 merger with Exelon — brings investment banking and utility-CEO pedigree to the board that is unusual even by the standards of large-cap power-sector governance.

## Financial Baseline

The earnings expansion from the 2022 spin baseline through fiscal 2025 reflects a convergence of structural forces rather than a single cyclical year. Constellation reported fiscal 2024 revenue of approximately $23.6 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of approximately $4.8 billion — up substantially from $3.8 billion in fiscal 2023 — as the first full year of IRA Section 45U production tax credits flowed through the income statement alongside elevated PJM capacity prices. Adjusted operating earnings of $8.67 per share exceeded the company's twice-revised guidance ceiling of $8.40. By fiscal 2025, revenue had expanded to approximately $25.5 billion, and adjusted operating earnings reached $9.39 per share, driven by continued 45U credit capture, higher capacity revenue, and the initial contribution of the Calpine acquisition in the fourth quarter. Writing alongside the February 2026 earnings release, Dominguez was direct: "Constellation enters 2026 well positioned to meet the nation's growing demand for reliable, clean electricity."

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA | Adj. EPS |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $24.4bn | $2.7bn | — |
| FY2023 | $23.6bn | $3.8bn | — |
| FY2024 | ~$23.6bn | ~$4.8bn | $8.67 |
| FY2025 | ~$25.5bn | — | $9.39 |

*Sources: [Constellation FY2024 press release](https://www.constellationenergy.com/newsroom/2025/constellation-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results.html); [FY2025 results, StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/CEG/constellation-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-sblgu0ybac63.html); prep data financials.json.*

## The IRA Floor

The Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45U production tax credit for existing nuclear generation is the structural element that remade the investment thesis. The credit provides up to $15 per megawatt-hour on qualifying zero-emission nuclear output, with a phase-out above an effective gross-receipts threshold of approximately $25 per megawatt-hour, running through 2032. In practical terms, the 45U credit functions as a revenue floor: at depressed spot power prices, the credit steps in to support a minimum effective realisation, dramatically reducing the commodity downside that had weighed on merchant nuclear operators throughout the 2010s. Combined with the PJM Interconnection's 2025–2026 capacity auction, which cleared above $269 per megawatt-day for most of the footprint, reflecting AI data centre load growth and tightening reserve margins, the two-sided revenue structure transformed the risk-return profile of Constellation's nuclear fleet into something closer to a contracted utility than a pure commodity-exposed merchant generator.

## A Second Hyperscaler

The Microsoft PPA at Crane established the commercial template; the second proof of concept arrived on June 3, 2025, when Constellation announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Meta Platforms for 1,121 megawatts from the Clinton Clean Energy Center in Illinois — a plant whose Illinois zero-emissions credit support was set to expire, placing it at decommissioning risk. The Meta agreement, which includes a 30-megawatt expansion of the facility and is expected to begin delivering power in June 2027, effectively converted a distressed asset into a contracted baseload resource with a hyperscaler counterparty. Meta's head of global energy, Urvi Parekh, described the rationale plainly:

> "Securing clean, reliable energy is necessary to continue advancing our AI ambitions."

The deal is also projected to preserve more than 1,000 Clinton jobs and generate approximately $13.5 million in annual tax revenue for the surrounding community — details that smooth regulatory pathways and reinforce the political durability of the nuclear revival. [Source: [ESG Dive](https://www.esgdive.com/news/meta-constellation-illinois-clinton-nuclear-ppa-support-ai-goals/749965/); [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/03/meta-signs-nuclear-power-deal-with-constellation-energy-.html)]

## The Calpine Acquisition

While the hyperscaler PPA strategy was taking shape, Constellation simultaneously moved to transform its generation platform in size and fuel mix. On January 10, 2025, the company announced an agreement to acquire Calpine Corporation — the largest private power producer in the United States — for approximately $26.6 billion in total consideration, comprising roughly $16.4 billion in cash, approximately 50 million newly issued CEG shares, and the assumption of approximately $12.7 billion in Calpine net debt. Calpine's approximately 27-gigawatt fleet — weighted heavily toward gas-fired combined-cycle generation plus The Geysers geothermal complex in California — provided the dispatchable complement to Constellation's baseload nuclear portfolio, along with geographic reach into ERCOT and CAISO that the nuclear-concentrated legacy footprint lacked. The transaction closed on February 20, 2026, following FERC and other regulatory approvals, creating the largest electricity generator in the United States by installed capacity: approximately 55 gigawatts serving approximately 2.5 million customers across the major US power markets. [Source: [247 Wall St.](https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/02/25/nuclear-giant-constellation-closes-calpine-deal-while-retail-investors-lose-faith/); [Constellation IR](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-acquire-calpine-creates-americas-leading-producer)]

## The Central Question

At a market capitalisation of approximately $107 billion to $112 billion as of early 2026 — up from roughly $13.7 billion at the February 2022 spin, a compound annual growth rate exceeding 69 percent — Constellation trades on the convergence of three secular tailwinds: AI data centre electricity demand, the IRA 45U production tax credit floor, and the structural repricing of PJM capacity margins. The Crane restart targets 835 megawatts of contracted hyperscaler output around 2028; the Meta PPA extended the model to a second plant in a different ISO; and Calpine added dispatchable gas and geothermal scale. The questions this dossier works through from this baseline are three: whether the hyperscaler-PPA template can be replicated across the remaining uncontracted nuclear fleet on terms that convert baseload capacity into multi-decade contracted cash flows; what the Calpine integration ultimately delivers in margin expansion and capital allocation optionality; and how durable the AI-driven electricity demand cycle proves to be — and at what earnings multiple that durability commands.

chapters.title: From the 2012 Exelon merger through the 2022 spin to the AI inflection
chapters.body:
## Two Companies Before the Merger

Long before the corporate separation that created today's Constellation Energy Corporation, two distinct utilities occupied adjacent but strategically divergent positions in American power markets.

In Baltimore, Constellation Energy Group stood as the holding company for Baltimore Gas and Electric, a century-old regulated utility serving Maryland's central corridor, alongside one of the country's most aggressive competitive merchant-generation and retail-energy supply businesses. Under Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Mayo A. Shattuck III — a former Alex. Brown investment banker who had become one of the more commercially sophisticated utility chiefs of his era — the Baltimore company had built a national footprint in wholesale power, structured energy products, and retail supply far beyond what a BGE parent alone would have justified.

In Chicago, Exelon Corporation had assembled the country's largest nuclear fleet through its own 2000 merger of PECO Energy and Unicom Corporation, the ComEd parent. Under Chief Executive John Rowe — a methodical, legally trained utility executive who had built Exelon into the dominant US nuclear operator — the company had systematically expanded its reactor portfolio while managing the political complexity that came with operating in Illinois, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and the broader Mid-Atlantic.

## The 2012 Merger: Exelon Acquires Constellation Energy Group

The rationale that Rowe and Shattuck assembled publicly in 2011 and early 2012 was straightforward: an Exelon-Constellation combination would create the largest utility company in the United States by customer count, combine the nuclear fleets under a single operator, and integrate Constellation's competitive supply capabilities into Exelon's broader structure.

The merger was not frictionless. Maryland regulators extracted customer-rate protections before approving the transaction. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission also required structural commitments before clearing the deal.

The merger closed in March 2012. Exelon acquired Constellation Energy Group in a stock-for-stock transaction. Shattuck did not remain as a senior executive in the combined company. Rowe retired shortly after the merger closed, handing the CEO role to Christopher Crane, the nuclear-operations veteran who had run Exelon Nuclear.

## A Difficult Decade: Merchant Nuclear Under Pressure

What followed over the next decade was a sustained compression of the merchant nuclear model. From 2012 through the late 2010s, the expansion of natural-gas-fired generation — enabled by the shale revolution — depressed wholesale power prices in PJM and MISO, squeezing the economics of baseload nuclear plants whose operating costs were largely fixed. Several of Exelon's older, smaller single-unit reactors operated below cash breakeven through multiple years of the 2015-2019 trough.

Exelon's response was twofold: aggressive engagement with state legislators and regulators in Illinois and New York to secure zero-emissions credits for nuclear plants that might otherwise close, and a growing internal debate about the optimal corporate structure. The Illinois Future Energy Jobs Act of 2016 and the New York Clean Energy Standard kept several plants operating that might otherwise have been retired. But the regulatory patchwork was state-specific and partial.

## February 2022: The Separation

By the early 2020s, Exelon management had concluded that the regulated utility business and the merchant-generation business had fundamentally divergent profiles: different capital structures, different investor bases, different regulatory regimes. A single holding company serving both constituencies was suboptimal for each.

The separation plan envisioned spinning off Constellation Energy Corporation as a standalone publicly traded company. Exelon would retain the six regulated utility businesses: ComEd (Illinois), PECO (Pennsylvania), BGE (Maryland), ACE (New Jersey), Pepco (Washington, DC), and Delmarva Power. The nuclear fleet and the Constellation competitive supply business would transfer to the new entity.

The spin-off economics at inception were not particularly flattering to Constellation. The company entered the public markets as a merchant nuclear operator at a moment when nuclear generation was not yet broadly understood as a scarce resource with strategic value. The equity was priced accordingly.

## The IRA and the Nuclear Re-Rating

The August 2022 passage of the Inflation Reduction Act changed that calculus structurally. The significance of the Section 45U PTC was not merely incremental revenue — it was the elimination of the downside scenario that had made merchant nuclear economics so painful in the 2015-2019 trough. At low wholesale power prices, the credit would offset revenue shortfall, creating an effective floor on nuclear plant economics. Analysts and investors began to price this structural shift into the equity through 2023 and 2024.

## Three Mile Island and the Hyperscaler Template

The September 2024 Microsoft PPA crystallised what the equity had been pricing in the abstract. The plant had been shut down in September 2019 for economic reasons, unable to compete in the PJM wholesale market without structural policy support. The combination of the IRA Section 45U credit framework and the price Microsoft committed in a 20-year bilateral agreement changed the restart economics. The transaction demonstrated that hyperscale data-centre operators would pay long-term contracted prices for firm clean baseload power that exceeded the PJM spot clearing price.

## Calpine and the Platform Extension

The January 2025 Calpine acquisition extended the platform beyond nuclear into a diversified merchant generation company. Calpine's fleet provided dispatch flexibility and peak capacity in markets where Constellation had limited presence, particularly ERCOT. The Geysers added firm renewable generation with a resource profile distinct from wind or solar. The combined platform would be one of the largest merchant generation companies in US history.

---

Constellation Energy entered the post-spin era as a merchant nuclear company at a trough valuation. By fiscal 2024, the company had been re-rated as the principal scaled US nuclear pure-play in an environment where AI data-centre load growth had transformed the supply-demand balance. The arc from Mayo Shattuck's Baltimore merchant house through the Exelon decade to Joe Dominguez's nuclear pure-play had taken fourteen years to complete — and had arrived at a moment when nuclear generation's structural scarcity became the most valuable attribute in American power markets.

chapters.title: Nuclear fleet, gas-and-renewables generation, and competitive supply
chapters.body:
## A two-segment business

At the broadest level, Constellation operates in two principal segments: Generation, encompassing nuclear, gas, hydro, wind, and solar production facilities, and Customer Channels, the competitive retail and wholesale supply business serving commercial, industrial, and residential customers in deregulated electricity markets. The Calpine acquisition adds a third dimension — dispatchable gas-fired generation and geothermal capacity — that reshapes the company's dispatch stack. [Constellation Energy 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001868275](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001868275)

## The nuclear fleet

The Generation segment is anchored by the largest commercial nuclear fleet in the United States, concentrated in the mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions within PJM and MISO, with additional capacity in NYISO and ISO-NE.

The Illinois units — Byron, Braidwood, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle, and Quad Cities — represent the densest cluster by geography. Calvert Cliffs in Maryland and Limerick and Peach Bottom in Pennsylvania serve the PJM mid-Atlantic zone. Ginna and Nine Mile Point anchor the New York portfolio within NYISO. The Peach Bottom and Salem units are partially owned, reflecting legacy consortium structures typical of plants built in the 1970s and 1980s.

Alongside the nuclear fleet, the Generation segment includes gas-fired peakers, combined-cycle assets, run-of-river hydroelectric capacity, wind, and utility-scale solar. These non-nuclear assets provide dispatch flexibility and hedging capability but remain secondary to the nuclear portfolio by a wide margin.

## Licence renewals and the 80-year nuclear horizon

A structural feature distinguishing Constellation's fleet is the multi-decade licence runway secured through NRC-approved renewals. Nuclear plants are initially licensed for 40 years; the NRC's first renewal programme extended authorisations to 60 years, and subsequent-licence-renewal applications pursue extensions to 80 years.

By the snapshot date, several units had received or were pursuing second licence renewals. The 80-year authorisations fundamentally alter long-term earnings visibility — a reactor licensed to operate through the 2050s or 2060s is an asset of different economic character than one facing closure within a decade. For investors building DCF models, the licence tail is among the highest-leverage inputs.

## Section 45U mechanics in practice

At the PJM and broader merchant power-market price levels prevailing through 2023-2025 — elevated by the power-commodity cycle and AI data-centre load growth — most Constellation nuclear units generated revenue above the 45U phase-out threshold, leaving the credit only partially in the money. The PTC's function is architectural rather than immediate: at lower-price periods, the credit engages to support a minimum effective price, converting what was historically open-ended downside exposure into a partial floor structure.

> "The IRA fundamentally changed the risk-return profile of nuclear," Dominguez told investors. "We have a floor we didn't have before."

## Customer Channels: competitive retail and wholesale supply

The Customer Channels segment operates Constellation's competitive retail electricity and gas supply business, serving C&I customers across deregulated markets including Texas, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, and Maryland. The wholesale power and load-serving activities provide a proprietary position in structured power products — a capability that became commercially important as hyperscalers began seeking bespoke multi-decade PPAs.

The segment serves as the commercial interface between the generation fleet and end-load customers. The retail and wholesale book provides a natural hedge on a portion of nuclear output, reducing the proportion sold at spot market prices. The ability to originate and structure bilateral PPAs became the scaffolding on which the hyperscaler PPA pipeline was built.

## The Calpine platform extension

Calpine brings capacity concentrated in ERCOT (Texas), CAISO (California), and ISO-NE — geographies where Constellation's existing nuclear footprint was limited or absent. The portfolio includes The Geysers geothermal complex, approximately 725 megawatts of firm renewable baseload constituting the largest geothermal facility in the United States.

The gas-fired fleet provides dispatchable capacity complementing nuclear baseload — a critical attribute for hyperscaler customers requiring guaranteed around-the-clock power delivery. The geographic diversification extends Constellation into markets experiencing the most acute AI-driven load growth. The Geysers adds firm, zero-carbon generation that commands a premium from corporate offtakers.

| Segment | Capacity (approx.) | Primary markets | Generation type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nuclear (standalone CEG) | ~22 GW | PJM, MISO, NYISO, ISO-NE | Nuclear baseload |
| Non-nuclear generation (standalone CEG) | Multiple GW | PJM, MISO | Gas, hydro, wind, solar |
| Calpine (pro-forma addition) | ~27 GW + 725 MW geothermal | ERCOT, CAISO, ISO-NE | Gas-fired CC/peakers, geothermal |

## Hyperscaler PPA pipeline

The Microsoft PPA established the commercial template. In subsequent earnings communications, Dominguez indicated the transaction catalysed active dialogue with additional hyperscaler customers for structured nuclear output agreements. Each hyperscaler agreement layers contracted revenue onto the fleet's merchant book, progressively shifting the earnings profile from commodity-price volatility toward multi-decade visibility — a transformation that, combined with the 45U floor, reshapes how investors assign terminal value to the nuclear fleet.

chapters.title: $23.6B revenue, $4.8B adjusted EBITDA, and the AI re-rating
chapters.body:
## The margin revolution: EBITDA doubles in three years

Constellation Energy closed fiscal 2024 with revenue of approximately $23.6 billion and adjusted EBITDA of approximately $4.8 billion — a figure that, measured against the $2.7 billion posted in the company's first full year as a standalone public entity, represented a near-doubling of operating profitability across three fiscal years. That expansion occurred on a revenue base that was effectively flat, a dynamic that encapsulates the structural shift in Constellation's earnings architecture since the February 2022 Exelon spin.

Revenue was slightly lower in 2024 than in 2022, yet adjusted EBITDA was nearly 80% higher. The explanation lies in the confluence of three structural forces: the Section 45U production tax credit, the dramatic repricing of PJM capacity auction results, and the broader merchant power cycle that tightened reserve margins across the eastern interconnect.

## The 45U PTC: engineering a price floor

At the fleet's historical capacity factor of approximately 95%, implied annual generation runs in the range of 180 to 190 terawatt-hours. At the full $15 per MWh rate, the theoretical maximum annual credit value would be approximately $2.7 billion to $2.9 billion — a figure that contextualises the EBITDA step-up, even as the realised credit is modulated by prevailing power prices.

Prior to the IRA, the merchant nuclear fleet operated with no floor on power price exposure. Nuclear plants carrying 40 to 45 percent of their cost base as fixed expense were structurally at risk of margin compression in low-gas-price environments. The 45U credit converts that risk profile: a sustained decline below the phase-out threshold triggers an increased credit value, partially or fully offsetting revenue compression. CFO Eggers described the PTC as providing the earnings predictability that allowed Constellation to pursue long-term capital commitments that would have been difficult to underwrite against an unhedged merchant revenue base.

## PJM capacity: the auction that changed the arithmetic

The July 2024 PJM capacity auction for the 2025-2026 delivery year cleared at over $269 per megawatt-day — a step-change from prior years reflecting AI data centre load growth, thermal capacity retirements, and revised demand forecasts. Constrained zones, including portions of the Midwest where Constellation's Illinois units are concentrated, cleared higher still.

For Constellation's PJM nuclear fleet, the capacity revenue uplift at $269-plus per MW-day is measured in hundreds of millions of dollars of incremental annual revenue. Capacity revenue is contractually locked for the 12-month delivery period, providing earnings certainty that complements longer-duration energy hedges. This channel captures hyperscaler demand surge before any bilateral PPA is negotiated.

## The PPA economics

The economics of the Microsoft PPA were not publicly disclosed in SEC filings, but industry analysis from S&P Global Market Intelligence and Platts estimated the implied effective power price at $100 to $115 per MWh — substantially above prevailing PJM day-ahead levels.

At $100 per MWh on 835 megawatts running at a 95% capacity factor, annual revenue from the Crane facility would reach approximately $700 million against a $1.6 billion capital investment — an asset-level revenue payback period of roughly two to three years before operating costs and financing charges. The PPA provides contracted revenue certainty that insulates project economics from both PJM spot volatility and the 45U phase-out dynamic.

## Calpine: financing the extension

To finance the cash component, Constellation arranged committed bridge facilities with the intention to refinance through investment-grade term debt and operating cash flow. The equity component, at roughly 50 million shares, represented meaningful dilution but was sized to maintain the investment-grade credit profile — a non-negotiable condition given the scale of ongoing capital commitments.

## Capital allocation

Through 2022-2024, Constellation deployed capital across three channels: common dividend initiated post-spin, share repurchase programmes, and the TMI restart alongside sustaining investment across the fleet.

Acquisition financing curtailed near-term buyback capacity, and bridge facility covenants imposed short-term leverage constraints. Eggers indicated the capital allocation framework would normalise following close, with the combined company's free cash profile expected to support resumed capital returns at scale.

---

The fiscal 2024 EBITDA was the arithmetic consequence of three layered structural forces acting simultaneously: the IRA price floor through 45U, capacity market repricing driven by AI load, and the hyperscaler PPA premium. The question that had hung over the post-spin equity — whether the largest US nuclear fleet could be transformed into a high-margin, contractually anchored clean energy infrastructure asset — had been substantially answered in the affirmative.

chapters.title: From the 2022 post-spin baseline to the 2024 record and Calpine
chapters.body:
## Standing Alone: Q1 2022 and the Post-Spin Thesis

Dominguez used the first post-spin earnings cycle to frame what Constellation was, and what it was not. The company was not a regulated utility earning a predictable return on equity. It was a merchant generator in a competitive wholesale market — a distinction the pre-IRA nuclear sector had spent a decade being punished for. The clean-energy baseload thesis held that nuclear output was, by output volume, the largest source of carbon-free electricity in the United States, and the policy environment was tilting in its favour.

Revenue in fiscal 2022 reached $24.4 billion, reflecting the elevated power-price environment as European natural gas dislocations rippled through US wholesale electricity markets. The pre-IRA merchant nuclear model required power prices to remain elevated to justify continued operation of older units. That constraint was about to be removed.

## The IRA and the 45U Floor

Constellation's hedging and operating teams spent the second half of 2022 and much of 2023 working through implementation mechanics with Treasury. The financial trajectory through fiscal 2023 reflected the early harvest of the re-rating: revenue came in at $23.6 billion, while adjusted EBITDA jumped to $3.8 billion — an increase of more than forty percent over the 2022 baseline. The EBITDA expansion in the face of flat revenue revealed the operating-leverage dynamic at work.

By Q4 2023 results, the AI narrative was surfacing explicitly in earnings commentary. The hyperscaler demand thesis had circulated in analyst circles for several quarters, and Constellation was fielding inbound interest from potential counterparties.

## September 2024: The Microsoft Transaction

The transaction was transformative on several dimensions. It demonstrated that a hyperscaler would commit to a twenty-year nuclear power contract — an instrument without precedent in US commercial nuclear history. It validated the carbon-free, around-the-clock premium that nuclear commands over intermittent renewables for data centre customers operating against Science Based Targets. And it established a template — long tenor, take-or-pay economics, investment-grade counterparty — that the commercial organisation under Chief Commercial Officer James McHugh could reference in every subsequent negotiation. [Constellation Energy IR](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/financial-information)

In Q3 2024 earnings commentary, Dominguez characterised the transaction as a defining moment not merely for Constellation but for the US nuclear industry broadly. The market agreed: CEG shares re-rated materially through the second half of 2024, making Constellation one of the best-performing US large-cap equities of the year.

## FY2024 Record Results and the Calpine Announcement

The Q4 2024 and full-year earnings release confirmed the scale of the earnings inflection. Full-year 2024 revenue held flat at $23.6 billion while adjusted EBITDA reached $4.8 billion — an increase of roughly $1.0 billion over the prior year and nearly double the 2022 baseline.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adj. EBITDA (USD bn) | EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 (first full post-spin year) | 24.4 | 2.7 | 11.1% |
| 2023 | 23.6 | 3.8 | 16.1% |
| 2024 | 23.6 | 4.8 | 20.3% |

The margin expansion was the product of three reinforcing forces: the 45U PTC floor, the elevated PJM capacity market clearing, and the initial commercial premium embedded in the hyperscaler PPA structure.

The strategic logic of the Calpine acquisition was both defensive and offensive. Dispatchable gas-fired capacity addressed a structural criticism of the pure-play nuclear model: nuclear is baseload, not peaking. Adding Calpine strengthened the product offering to hyperscaler customers seeking round-the-clock reliability plus peak-hour coverage. ERCOT and CAISO exposure diversified away from PJM concentration.

## 2025 and the Broadening Pipeline

Through 2025 and into Q1 2026, earnings communications focused on three themes: Calpine integration progress, the broadening hyperscaler PPA pipeline, and ongoing Section 45U realisation. Dominguez framed the combined platform as a uniquely comprehensive US merchant power portfolio capable of meeting the full spectrum of hyperscaler electricity needs.

Eggers's communications addressed the credit's interaction with the growing PPA portfolio — specifically, how contracted prices above the phase-out threshold affected the realised value of the 45U floor at individual plants as the fleet's effective blended price continued to rise with each incremental agreement.

The earnings arc from the 2022 baseline through Q1 2026 described a company that had navigated from an uncertain merchant survivor into the principal equity instrument for the AI data centre electricity investment thesis. EBITDA had nearly doubled across two fiscal years, the Microsoft PPA had unlocked a replicable commercial template, and the Calpine acquisition had elevated the company into a categorically different scale class.

chapters.title: Dominguez, Shattuck, Eggers, and the nuclear-operator board
chapters.body:
## Dominguez at the helm: the CEO mandate

Joseph Dominguez inherited a peculiar mandate at the spin: build a coherent identity for a company that was simultaneously the largest US nuclear fleet operator, a competitive retail electricity supplier, and a merchant generation business whose earnings were structurally correlated to commodity power prices.

Dominguez was a natural fit. A mechanical engineer from the New Jersey Institute of Technology, he later took a law degree *magna cum laude* from Rutgers before serving as an assistant US attorney in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. His energy career was built at Exelon across regulatory and government affairs — he served as EVP for governmental and regulatory affairs before becoming chief executive of ComEd, Exelon's Illinois T&D subsidiary serving more than four million customers.

What the ComEd tenure gave Dominguez was precisely the stakeholder management and political engagement that merchant power generation requires. Nuclear relicensing, capacity market design advocacy at FERC, state zero-emission credit programmes, and ultimately the IRA Section 45U negotiation — all involved the same combination of regulatory command and political coalition-building that had defined his regulated-utility years. At the September 2024 Microsoft announcement, Dominguez articulated the commercial thesis:

> "The agreement marks the dawn of a new era of nuclear energy. It demonstrates nuclear's capability to meet the demands of our modern economy and confirms our belief that nuclear energy is essential to a clean energy future."

## The CFO function: Eggers, Smith, and the capital structure trajectory

Daniel Eggers's background was unusual among utility CFOs: approximately eighteen years at Credit Suisse, where he co-headed US energy equity research, before moving to Exelon's IR and corporate finance function. That analytical heritage made him an unusually adept communicator — in three consecutive years he won [Institutional Investor](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com)'s best CFO award for the utilities sector (2023, 2024, and 2025).

With the Calpine close, Eggers transitioned to Senior Executive Vice President for Finance and Data Economy — a title acknowledging both the expanded balance sheet and emerging AI data centre energy ambitions. Shane Smith, who had spent twenty years in the finance organisation and led treasury through the Calpine deal structuring, ascended to the CFO seat.

## The operational core

Bryan Hanson, as Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Generation Officer, carries the company's largest single operational responsibility: the safe and reliable operation of more than 170 generating units coast-to-coast. Hanson's career was spent almost entirely within nuclear operations — beginning at the plant level, extending through fleet-wide oversight at Exelon Nuclear, and reaching the executive position now encompassing the post-Calpine portfolio. He chaired the 2025 American Nuclear Society Annual Conference.

James McHugh, as Chief Commercial Officer, runs the organisation through which the hyperscaler PPA framework was developed. McHugh previously served as CEO of the Constellation subsidiary within Exelon Generation and held senior wholesale trading roles dating to the early Exelon Power Team years. His team manages wholesale hedging across PJM, MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE and builds the pipeline of hyperscaler engagements.

Kathleen Barron, as Executive Vice President and Senior Advisor to the CEO, brought thirty years of energy policy and regulatory law. She served as Deputy General Counsel at FERC before joining Constellation's predecessor in 2010. Her fifteen years in government affairs made her the principal architect of the engagement that contributed to the IRA nuclear provisions. Barron announced plans to retire in 2026.

David Dardis, as Chief External Affairs and Growth Officer, combines legal leadership with new development. He served as legal adviser to FERC Chairman Joseph Kelliher during the Energy Policy Act of 2005 implementation before joining in 2007. His nearly two decades encompassed complex M&A execution including Calpine, major contract negotiations, and national energy policy advocacy.

## The board: expertise calibrated to a merchant nuclear business

The Constellation Energy board assembled at the February 2022 spin carried a disciplined composition logic: technical nuclear expertise, financial markets depth, large industrial operating experience, and regulatory familiarity — with none of the conventions that typically dominate a regulated transmission-and-distribution company's governance structure.

**Robert J. Lawless** served as non-executive Chairman, and his tenure with the Constellation enterprise was longer than virtually any other current board member. Lawless had first joined the Constellation Energy Group board in 2002 — a full decade before the original group merged into Exelon — and had continued on the Exelon board through the 2022 separation, arriving at the new CEG as Chairman at inception. His operating career was as Chairman, President, and CEO of McCormick & Company, the Fortune 500 spice and flavoring manufacturer: a background that brought large-enterprise operational governance discipline rather than sector-specific nuclear expertise, paired with twenty-plus years of direct institutional memory of the Constellation and Exelon nuclear-fleet businesses across multiple market cycles.

**Yves C. de Balmann** brought the deepest capital markets pedigree on the board. He served as Co-Head of Deutsche Bank's Global Investment Bank and as Co-Chairman and Co-CEO of BT Alex. Brown — the bulge-bracket investment banking operation within Bankers Trust — before building Bregal Investments, a private equity platform for the Brenninkmeijer family, from inception to more than €18 billion in assets under management. Critically, de Balmann also served on the original Constellation Energy Group board from 2003 to 2012, giving him direct prior exposure to the merchant nuclear business before it became part of Exelon. He chaired the Compensation Committee and sat on Corporate Governance. As the company navigated the Calpine financing structure, the hyperscaler PPA economics, and the evolving capital return programme, his transactional and capital markets depth was structurally relevant in ways that few other board members could replicate.

**Admiral John M. Richardson** provided the board's most direct nuclear technical oversight. Richardson served as the 31st Chief of Naval Operations — the highest-ranking officer in the US Navy — and before that as Director of Naval Reactors, the position responsible for the full life-cycle management and regulatory compliance of more than ninety reactors aboard nuclear-powered warships. The combination of engineering credentials (physics at the Naval Academy; electrical engineering at MIT and Woods Hole) with regulatory experience managing a naval nuclear fleet larger than any commercial operator made him uniquely qualified to chair the Nuclear Oversight Committee — the standing committee with direct responsibility over Constellation's fleet safety programme.

**Dhiaa Jamil** complemented Richardson's credentials with commercial utility nuclear operations experience. Jamil spent forty-one years at Duke Energy, rising to Chief Nuclear Officer overseeing the largest regulated nuclear fleet in the country before serving as Chief Operating Officer until his 2023 retirement. His direct management of the Duke-Progress Energy nuclear integration — twelve units across two organisations — provided a merger-integration reference that was relevant as Constellation absorbed the Calpine fleet. He served on both the Compensation and Nuclear Oversight committees.

**Bradley M. Halverson** chaired the Audit and Risk Committee. His operating background was as Group President and CFO of Caterpillar — a Fortune 100 capital-intensive industrial company with global treasury, financial reporting, and risk management complexity. His public accounting origins at Price Waterhouse, combined with his ongoing audit committee chairmanship at Sysco Corporation, provided technical financial governance depth.

**Charles L. Harrington** served as Corporate Governance Committee Chair with a career that combined engineering and technology leadership with large organisation management. As Chairman, CEO, and President of Parsons Corporation, he oversaw cybersecurity, national security contracting, and complex critical infrastructure programmes directly relevant to Constellation's nuclear regulatory environment and broader infrastructure positioning.

**Julie Holzrichter** brought risk management and large-scale systems experience from her decade as Chief Operating Officer of CME Group, the world's leading derivatives marketplace. Operational risk, regulatory compliance, technology platform management, and the integration of multiple multi-billion-dollar exchange acquisitions during her CME tenure mapped onto Constellation's trading, retail, and risk management businesses.

**Ashish Khandpur** joined the board from a career in advanced materials and industrial technology, including the Research and Development leadership and CTO role at 3M Corporation, and subsequently the CEO and Chairman position at Avient Corporation. His innovation and technology orientation was increasingly relevant as Constellation sought to articulate its positioning in the AI data centre energy ecosystem.

**Eileen Paterson** arrived in December 2024 with aerospace and defence operating credentials — she had been CEO of Aerojet Rocketdyne, a major defence propulsion company — and brought a US Army aviation background that added an operational dimension distinct from the finance and industrial profiles elsewhere on the board. She served on the Nuclear Oversight and Corporate Governance committees.

**Nneka Rimmer** brought strategy consulting depth — fifteen years at Boston Consulting Group, where she became the firm's first Black female partner — alongside operational experience as President of McCormick's Global Flavors and Extracts division and chief transformation officer of the same business. Her M&A advisory and execution track record, including the largest acquisition in McCormick history, was directly applicable to a board overseeing a $26.6 billion integration.

## Composition thesis

Read as an ensemble, the board's composition reflected neither the regulatory-compact heritage of a traditional investor-owned utility nor the financial-engineering orientation of a private equity-backed merchant generator. It was instead calibrated to the specific demands of a post-2022 nuclear pure-play: technical oversight of an operationally complex and heavily regulated nuclear fleet (Richardson, Jamil, Paterson); financial and transactional governance of a merchant business with large capital market exposure (de Balmann, Halverson, Holzrichter); industrial operating depth (Harrington, Khandpur, Rimmer); and a Chairman in Lawless whose two decades of Constellation-enterprise board experience provided institutional continuity across every structural iteration of the business since the Constellation Energy Group's independent years. The Nuclear Oversight Committee — a standing committee with no equivalent on most large-cap corporate boards — was itself a structural statement about where the business's operational risks resided. The post-Calpine board carried the same logic, extended to a generation fleet that now encompassed gas and geothermal assets alongside the nuclear core that remained the earnings foundation.

chapters.title: Microsoft, hyperscalers, C&I customers, and the nuclear fuel cycle
chapters.body:
## The Crane Clean Energy Center: Updates Beyond the Template

The company subsequently accelerated its operational target to mid-2027, earlier than the original 2028 horizon, after the NRC indicated it expected to complete its licence review by 2027. In November 2025, the Trump administration deepened the federal backing: the Department of Energy closed a $1 billion conditional loan under the Title XVII clean-energy finance programme, with the first advance scheduled for Q1 2026, covering the majority of the restart capital outlay. The DOE described the transaction as the first project to achieve concurrent conditional commitment and financial close under the new administration, framing it explicitly as a national-security energy infrastructure investment.

Dominguez argued that hyperscalers required power that was simultaneously continuous, carbon-accountable, and physically located within the same grid region as their data centres:

> "Powering industries critical to our nation's global economic and technological competitiveness, including data centers, requires an abundance of energy that is carbon-free and reliable every hour of every day, and nuclear plants are the only energy sources that can consistently deliver on that promise."

## Meta and the Expanding Hyperscaler Pipeline

The Crane PPA proved to be the template rather than the exception. On June 3, 2025, Constellation and Meta announced a separate twenty-year power purchase agreement covering the full output of the Clinton Clean Energy Center in central Illinois — a 1,121-megawatt pressurised water reactor that had operated on state-funded zero-emission credits under Illinois's nuclear support programme. The ZEC framework, which had sustained the plant's economics through competitive electricity price weakness, was approaching expiration. The Meta agreement replaced the ratepayer-funded subsidy with a direct hyperscaler off-take commitment, extending Clinton's operating life by two decades on a purely market-based footing.

The Clinton PPA carries several structural features that illustrate how hyperscaler counterparties are adapting the standard corporate PPA format to nuclear baseload. The agreement begins in June 2027 — timed to the anticipated expiration of the ZEC contracts — and it incorporates a 30-megawatt capacity uprate at the plant, lifting total output above the original nameplate. Constellation estimated that the deal would preserve approximately 1,100 direct jobs at the Clinton site, contribute $13.5 million in annual local tax revenue, and include $1 million in community charitable commitments over five years. Dominguez characterised the agreement as "a model for how America's clean energy future can be driven by partnerships with forward-thinking companies."

Beyond Microsoft and Meta, Dominguez signalled in multiple earnings communications through 2025 that the hyperscaler dialogue had broadened materially. On the Q2 2025 call, he cited projections showing hyperscaler capital expenditure on data centre infrastructure for 2026 running approximately 75 percent above the prior year's pace. Constellation responded by submitting approximately 5,000 megawatts of new capacity resources into PJM's generation interconnection queue — a combination of nuclear uprates at existing plants, new natural gas peakers, and battery storage — positioning the fleet to serve additional off-take commitments as negotiations progressed. Dominguez noted a preference for announcing concluded data centre agreements in the presence of local community stakeholders rather than disclosing on earnings calls, suggesting additional executed PPAs may have preceded formal public announcement. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the Microsoft and Meta agreements represented the two publicly confirmed hyperscaler bilateral PPAs in Constellation's portfolio.

## PJM Capacity: Forward Visibility

The combination of retiring coal capacity, surging AI data centre load, and sluggish new-build entry has produced three consecutive capacity auction records in PJM. The 2026–2027 auction cleared at $329.17 per megawatt-day — a 22 percent increase over the 2025-2026 record — as PJM's forecast showed peak load rising by more than 5,400 megawatts year-on-year, driven by data centre expansion and industrial electrification. Constellation's nuclear units cleared 21 percent of PJM's total procured capacity.

The December 2025 auction for the 2027–2028 delivery year was particularly significant: the company disclosed in its 8-K filing that it had cleared approximately 17,950 megawatts, translating to approximately $2.2 billion in committed capacity revenues for that delivery year.

## Commercial and Industrial Supply: The Retail Foundation

At spin-off, the competitive supply business served approximately 140 terawatt-hours of electric power load and approximately 800 billion cubic feet of natural gas annually, principally to C&I customers across the deregulated Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Northeast.

The C&I customer base spans Fortune 100 manufacturers, hospital systems, universities, municipalities, and government entities. Constellation's value proposition combines physical supply from the nuclear fleet — zero-carbon baseload with demonstrable hourly matching — with the financial and structured products capacity of the competitive supply organisation. This retail channel operates in parallel to the hyperscaler PPA business, provides diversification of counterparty credit quality and tenor, and serves as a commercial intelligence channel offering early visibility into load-growth signals from manufacturing expansions and mid-tier data centre operators.

## The Nuclear Fuel Cycle: Concentration, Geopolitics, and the Russian Equation

Operating the largest US nuclear fleet generates a procurement footprint that extends from the uranium mines of Kazakhstan, Canada, and Australia through conversion plants, enrichment facilities, and fuel fabrication shops before arriving at the reactor core. Each stage of the fuel cycle carries its own supply-concentration risk, and the geopolitical dislocation triggered by Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine threw the enrichment segment specifically into relief.

Russian state-controlled enrichment capacity, operated through Rosatom's TENEX and TVEL subsidiaries, had supplied approximately 20 percent of enriched uranium delivered to US reactors as recently as 2024, reflecting long-term supply contracts negotiated over decades. The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act, signed into law on May 13, 2024, established a statutory ban on imports of Russian-origin low-enriched uranium, effective 90 days after enactment — approximately August 2024 — while authorising the Department of Energy to grant national-interest waivers through 2028 where no alternative supply was available. Constellation Energy, alongside Centrus Energy, was among the entities that secured such waivers, reflecting the material time required to redirect enrichment requirements to Western suppliers.

The Western enrichment landscape is effectively a three-provider oligopoly: Centrus Energy (formerly USEC), which operates the American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio; Urenco, a British-German-Dutch consortium with US enrichment capacity at the Louisiana Energy Services facility in New Mexico; and Orano (formerly Areva), a French state-backed group with global enrichment infrastructure. Centrus has been scaling domestic centrifuge manufacturing with backing from the Department of Energy's civil nuclear programme and a February 2025 supply contract with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power; it delivered over 920 kilograms of high-assay low-enriched uranium to the DOE through mid-2025 as part of a demonstration programme for next-generation reactor fuel.

The downstream fuel fabrication step — where enriched uranium hexafluoride is converted into ceramic pellets and assembled into fuel assemblies — is dominated in the US by Westinghouse Electric Company, which supplies light-water reactor fuel for Constellation's pressurised and boiling water units, and by Framatome (formerly Areva NP), which serves portions of the fleet. Both fabricators maintained continuity of supply through the Russian import disruption period, drawing on enrichment inventories and diversified enrichment contracts. For Constellation, the practical effect of the Russian ban and waiver regime is a managed transition over the 2024–2028 window toward Western-sourced enrichment, with contract re-tendering that carries an incremental cost increase relative to the historical Russian price points. The company's scale — operating 21-plus reactors — gives it negotiating leverage with Western enrichers and fabricators that smaller operators cannot replicate, though it also means the absolute dollar exposure to enrichment price escalation is proportionally larger.

The geopolitical overlay on the fuel cycle connects directly to the broader policy environment in which Constellation operates: the IRA Section 45U production tax credit, the federal loan support for Crane, the Trump administration's explicit framing of nuclear expansion as a national security and AI competitiveness priority, and the NRC re-licensing infrastructure that underpins the restart timeline. Dominguez, speaking to Semafor in April 2026, warned that the US was not on track to "win" the race against China's AI energy build-out without more aggressive domestic energy deployment — a political argument that aligned Constellation's commercial interests with the national-interest framing that had unlocked federal support at each stage of the Crane project.

---

*Sources: [Constellation Energy IR — Microsoft PPA announcement, September 20 2024](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-and-microsoft-reach-agreement-restore-iconic-three); [Constellation Energy IR — Meta PPA announcement, June 3 2025](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-meta-sign-20-year-deal-clean-reliable-nuclear); [Utility Dive — DOE $1B loan, Crane restart](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/doe-loan-constellation-crane-nuclear-restart/805923/); [Utility Dive — PJM capacity prices record, 2024/25](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-interconnection-capacity-auction-data-center/808264/); [Utility Dive — PJM 2026/27 record $329/MW-day](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-interconnection-capacity-auction-prices/753798/); [Constellation Energy 8-K, PJM 2027/28 auction](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001868275/000186827525000112/ceg-20251217.htm); [DOE — Russian Uranium Ban](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/russian-uranium-ban-will-speed-development-us-nuclear-fuel-supply-chain); [Congress.gov — Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/1042/all-info); [Semafor — Dominguez on China AI race, April 2026](https://www.semafor.com/article/04/14/2026/constellation-energy-ceo-joe-dominguez-says-us-not-going-to-win-the-race-with-china-ai-energy-buildout)*

chapters.title: Where Constellation sits against Vistra, NRG, NextEra, and the IPP set
chapters.body:
## Scale Without Parallel

The Calpine close created something that had not previously existed in the American power sector: a single merchant generation company at a scale that dwarfed every competitive peer while holding the largest portfolio of zero-carbon baseload generation in the country. The combined entity produced a pro-forma fleet of approximately 49 gigawatts in competitive markets. No other independent power producer came close.

Understanding where the company sits requires mapping the full terrain of the US merchant generation and utility landscape, and interrogating whether the structural advantages are durable.

## The Merchant IPP Peer Group

The US competitive generation sector had, by the mid-2020s, consolidated around a handful of significant players following years of post-deregulation restructuring, several rounds of bankruptcy, and the more recent wave of AI-driven demand repricing.

| Company | Capacity (approx.) | Nuclear Exposure | Primary RTO Footprint | Public Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Constellation (post-Calpine) | ~49 GW | ~22 GW | PJM, MISO, NYISO, CAISO, ERCOT | NASDAQ: CEG |
| Vistra Energy | ~41 GW | ~6 GW | ERCOT, PJM | NYSE: VST |
| NRG Energy | ~18 GW | Minimal | ERCOT, PJM, broader US | NYSE: NRG |
| Talen Energy | ~13 GW | ~2.5 GW | PJM | NASDAQ: TLN |
| Calpine (pre-acquisition) | ~27 GW | None | CAISO, ERCOT, PJM | Private |

Vistra Energy was, prior to the Calpine transaction, the most direct comparable to Constellation among publicly traded merchant generators. The Dallas-based company operated approximately 41 gigawatts of generation across nuclear, natural gas, coal, solar, and battery storage assets, with its largest footprint in ERCOT — the Texas grid — supplemented by substantial PJM presence. Vistra's September 2023 acquisition of Energy Harbor added meaningful nuclear capacity: the Davis-Besse, Perry, and Beaver Valley plants contributed approximately six gigawatts of nuclear generation, giving Vistra a credible nuclear story to carry into hyperscaler PPA conversations. Vistra's ERCOT positioning also provided unique exposure to the Texas data centre buildout, where load growth from technology companies was straining the grid by 2024 and 2025. Yet Vistra's nuclear footprint — roughly six gigawatts against Constellation's 22 — remained structurally smaller, limiting the company's addressable capacity for long-duration zero-carbon contracted supply.

NRG Energy occupied a different competitive register. NRG's business model had shifted substantially toward competitive retail supply — the acquisition of Vivint Smart Home and the broader consumer and business services push — with generation increasingly serving a supporting role. NRG's nuclear exposure was minimal by comparison; the company was more comparable to a large retail electricity provider with generation assets than a nuclear-anchored merchant. The ERCOT and broader US footprint gave NRG scale in competitive retail, but it was not competing for hyperscaler nuclear PPAs in the same way as Constellation or Vistra.

Talen Energy, the smallest of the publicly traded merchant peer group, had nonetheless established a precedent of outsized competitive significance. The March 2024 announcement that Talen's Susquehanna nuclear facility in Pennsylvania had entered a data centre co-location agreement with Cumulus Data — subsequently acquired by Amazon — established the template for direct hyperscaler-to-nuclear-plant power delivery that Constellation would execute at scale seven months later. The Susquehanna-Cumulus-Amazon transaction demonstrated that a hyperscaler would pay a premium for firm zero-carbon nuclear electrons delivered directly at the plant fence, bypassing the transmission grid. When FERC subsequently intervened on co-location interconnection rules, the regulatory precedent mattered for Talen and Constellation alike. Talen's scale, however, constrained the broader opportunity; at approximately 13 gigawatts total capacity with a single large nuclear station, Talen could not offer the multi-plant, multi-region contracted supply that Constellation's 12-plant fleet enabled.

## The Nuclear-Fleet Structural Moat

The structural competitive advantage rests on one fact: nuclear baseload generation at 22 gigawatts of scale cannot be replicated. New nuclear construction carries capital costs and construction timelines that make near-term additions economically marginal in competitive markets. The fleet Constellation inherited from Exelon was the product of decades of capital investment, regulatory licensing, and operational workforce development constituting a durable barrier to entry.

Every existing nuclear operator benefits from the Section 45U mechanism. But the scale of Constellation's exposure makes it the single largest 45U beneficiary by a substantial margin. At a fleet capacity factor consistently above 90 percent, the aggregate megawatt-hour volumes subject to the 45U framework are structurally larger than any competitor's — installing a revenue floor beneath core earnings at a scale no peer can match.

## Regulated Utilities and the Adjacent Landscape

Placing Constellation within the broader US electric utility sector required distinguishing between merchant IPPs and regulated utilities — a distinction that drove materially different valuation frameworks and competitive dynamics.

NextEra Energy, the largest US regulated utility by market capitalisation, was not a direct Constellation competitor but provided the most relevant scaled context. NextEra operated Florida Power & Light as a vertically integrated regulated utility alongside NextEra Energy Resources, the largest US renewables developer with wind and solar assets across 40 states. NextEra's nuclear exposure ran to approximately 5.5 gigawatts across its regulated and merchant portfolios, placing it broadly comparable to Vistra post-Energy Harbor. NextEra's competitive renewables development platform — principally wind, solar, and storage — was the largest in the country, but firm zero-carbon baseload nuclear capacity was not NextEra's differentiating asset in the hyperscaler PPA conversation in the way it was for Constellation.

Duke Energy, Southern Company, and Dominion Energy operated within vertically integrated regulated utility frameworks where generation returns were set through state rate cases and not exposed to merchant power-price volatility. These companies held substantial nuclear generation portfolios — Duke's fleet across the Carolinas, Southern's Plant Vogtle units in Georgia, Dominion's positions in Virginia and Connecticut — but the regulated cost-of-service recovery model meant their nuclear assets were not available for merchant hyperscaler PPA contracting in the same manner. Duke and Southern were building new nuclear through the AP1000 programme; Southern's Unit 3 at Vogtle reached commercial operation in mid-2023, Unit 4 in late 2023, representing the first new US nuclear construction completion in over three decades. But those assets remained inside regulated rate base rather than merchant markets.

Pure-play renewables developers — NextEra Energy Resources, AES Corporation, Brookfield Renewable — occupied a category defined by intermittency. Wind and solar generation, while cost-competitive on a levelised basis, could not provide the 24-hour, 365-day firm carbon-free power that hyperscalers specified in their data centre supply requirements. AES and Brookfield could contract renewable megawatts at scale, but the product lacked the firm dispatchable characteristics that nuclear generation uniquely provided. This technical distinction drove the premium pricing embedded in Constellation's hyperscaler PPA economics relative to comparable renewable power purchase agreements.

## PJM Positioning and the Capacity Market Uplift

Constellation's geographic concentration in PJM provides a specific capacity market advantage diverging from Vistra's ERCOT-weighted profile. Constrained zones, notably in the Chicago metropolitan area where Constellation's Illinois nuclear fleet is concentrated, cleared at higher prices than the RTO average.

Vistra captures capacity revenue in PJM and ERCOT, but ERCOT's capacity market structure differs materially from PJM's administratively determined capacity product, and the recent PJM auction outcomes specifically rewarded Constellation's nuclear positioning.

## Hyperscaler PPA Execution as the Differentiating Variable

If nuclear-fleet scale and Section 45U exposure define the structural competitive position, the differentiating execution variable is the pace and terms of hyperscaler PPA contracting. Talen's March 2024 Susquehanna-Amazon co-location deal established the proof of concept; Constellation's Microsoft agreement established the template at scale.

The Microsoft deal demonstrated that Constellation, operating 12 nuclear plants rather than Talen's one, could sequence additional hyperscaler transactions across its portfolio — a pipeline optionality no peer possesses at equivalent scale. Vistra's six gigawatts of nuclear capacity across three plants in one RTO offers a materially smaller addressable pipeline than Constellation's 22 gigawatts across 12 plants in multiple RTOs.

## The Post-Calpine Strategic Position

The Calpine acquisition resolved the one structural gap in Constellation's competitive positioning: dispatchable capacity. Nuclear generation cannot ramp to meet short-duration demand spikes. Calpine's fleet provides the flexible capacity complement. Together, the combined entity can offer hyperscaler or large industrial customers a bundled solution — nuclear baseload plus gas-fired dispatchable backup plus renewable certificates — across multiple grid regions.

The pro-forma scale surpassed Vistra's approximately 41 gigawatts and established a new category in US merchant generation. The competitive question going forward is whether that scale advantage translates into durable return advantages, or whether the gas-fired assets dilute the nuclear pure-play thesis. The answer depends on three variables: hyperscaler PPA contracting pace, 45U framework durability through 2032 and beyond, and the broader merchant power cycle trajectory.

chapters.title: From the 2022 spin through TMI to the Calpine close
chapters.body:
## Event timeline summary

The equity opened to cautious reception at the February 2022 spin. Merchant nuclear operators carried an institutional stigma earned across a decade of impairments and plant closures. The critical policy variable — whether Congress would intervene to support existing nuclear economics — remained unresolved.

That question was answered six months later with the IRA. The EBITDA trajectory validates the sequence: $2.7 billion in 2022 (pre-45U), $3.8 billion in 2023 (enactment and anticipation), $4.8 billion in 2024 (first full qualifying year combined with rising power prices and AI demand pull).

## Three Mile Island: from closure to template

The backstory was a shutdown decision made five years before the company existed in its current form. In September 2019, Exelon announced the permanent closure of Three Mile Island Unit 1 — the 835-megawatt reactor that had operated since 1974. The economics were straightforward: low wholesale power prices, absent a state zero-emission credit programme, made continued operation untenable. Unit 1 shut down on September 20, 2019.

What changed over the following five years — the IRA 45U PTC, AI data centre operators as large-scale purchasers of firm clean electricity, and the growing recognition that the grid had too little firm capacity — meant the logic forcing shutdown was running in reverse by 2024.

The September 2024 announcement crystallised the monetisation model: Constellation was not merely a passive beneficiary of rising wholesale prices but an active counterparty capable of structuring decade-spanning bilateral contracts with the most creditworthy corporate buyers in the world. The hyperscaler PPA became the principal valuation narrative.

## Forward catalysts

From the snapshot date, the principal near-term catalysts fell into three clusters. The Calpine integration represented the most immediate EPS event. The Crane Clean Energy Center restart remained on the critical path for the Microsoft PPA revenue to flow. And the broader hyperscaler PPA pipeline represented the next leg of the valuation story.

NRC re-licensing milestones at individual plants — Dresden, Quad Cities, and others with licences approaching extension deadlines — carried their own catalytic weight, each successful extension extending the earnings duration of the relevant asset by twenty years.

|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue (USD bn) | 24.4 | 23.6 | 23.6 |
| Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) | 2.7 | 3.8 | 4.8 |
| Nuclear fleet capacity (GW) | ~22 | ~22 | ~22 |
| Key policy event | IRA signed (Aug) | 45U finalisation | 45U first full year |
| Key commercial event | CEG spin (Feb) | — | Microsoft PPA (Sep) |
